title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 31-35
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 31-35 of the ai-adoption series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why does a procurement-only inventory undercount the AI tools in use?
options: Tools bought on team cards, expensed individually, or bundled as upgrades never appear there
Procurement records list only the tools that passed a security review before they were purchased
Procurement systems delete the record once a subscription has been paid for in full
Free tools are left out because there is no purchase order for the system to record
questions.explanation: Buying now happens outside purchase orders and inside subscriptions the company already owns, so only charges, expense reports, and embedded tiers show what is really in use.

questions.question: Why group tools by job category rather than by feature list?
options: Job categories are simpler to count, which makes the whole inventory much shorter to compile
Job categories map to departments, so grouping by job assigns the cost automatically
Feature lists change too often for procurement to keep them current in the records
Vendors converge on features, so overlap shows up only when tools are grouped by job
questions.explanation: Features converge across vendors and suites cover many jobs badly, so grouping by the task a person is trying to finish is what exposes real overlap and orphans.

questions.question: Why end a redundant contract at its renewal date rather than immediately?
options: Vendors will not discuss a migration until the existing agreement has fully expired
A forced mid-contract switch pays twice for the same job and makes consolidation painful
Users need a full year to learn a replacement before the old tool can be removed
The renewal date is the only point at which a vendor is legally permitted to delete company data
questions.explanation: Contracts end on dates, which is when ending one is cheap and starting another is negotiable; cutting early means paying both vendors for the same work.

questions.question: Why buy fewer seats than the number of eligible employees at the start?
options: Eligibility is a permission, and a waitlist measures who actually intends to use the tool
Buying fewer seats lowers the per-seat price that the vendor is willing to offer
Eligible employees rarely want the tool, so most of them would never log in anyway
Seat counts must almost always stay below total headcount because of standard contract terms
questions.explanation: Adoption is a behavior while eligibility is only a permission, so buying to eligibility turns a behavior question into a sunk cost and removes the waitlist that shows which teams are pulling.

questions.question: What is the most important fact about seat contracts during a rollout?
options: Price per seat falls as the total number of seats in the contract grows larger
Adding seats mid-term is easy, while removing them is a negotiation
Annual commitments always renew automatically without any notice period
Consumption pricing removes the need to track which users are active
questions.explanation: The purchased count is effectively locked until renewal, so buying ahead of demand becomes a commitment that cannot easily be reversed.

questions.question: A program reports 720 users active in the last 30 days out of 1,000 assigned and calls that 72 percent adoption. What is wrong with that figure?
options: The measurement window is too short, so the figure understates how many people truly use the tool
Assigned seats undercount real access, so the true adoption rate is higher than reported
One number hides five layers, and the habitual count predicts whether a renewal is defensible
Adoption should be measured only once a year, at the point of contract renewal
questions.explanation: Each gap between purchased, assigned, enabled, active, and habitual has a different cause, so one figure over one window cannot say whether a renewal is justified.

questions.question: A program keeps onboarding new groups and reports a flat or falling aggregate adoption rate. Why can the aggregate fall while every group is improving?
options: New groups are counted twice in the base until their first quarter of use ends
New groups start below the running average, so each one pulls the blended rate down
Habit thresholds are redefined for every wave, so older figures stop being comparable
Managers hold back reporting for new joiners until onboarding is finished
questions.explanation: An aggregate rate blends people who are still forming a habit with people who already have one, so each new group drags the average down while its own retention improves. Plotting retention by group separates onboarding effects from a genuine decline.

questions.question: Two programs both show a flat aggregate trend. One has covered everyone whose work fits the tool, and the other has groups that fade after a strong start. What tells the two situations apart?
options: Whether the number of licensed seats grew faster than the headcount over the same period
Whether weekly active users moved above or below the median of their own history
Whether cohort curves converge on a shared level or descend further in later waves
Whether the value line improved while the activity count stayed flat
questions.explanation: A plateau caused by covering everyone whose work fits the tool shows groups settling at a similar level, while groups that keep decaying point to enablement that failed to land. The shapes differ, so the remedies differ.

questions.question: Adoption numbers fall sharply in one quarter. What order of investigation keeps the review from wasting time on the wrong explanation?
options: Rule out composition, window, instrument, and calendar effects before testing behavior
Open with a full strategy review, since several metrics moving together signals a program problem
Start with a user survey, because only the people using the tool can explain the drop
Begin with control chart limits, so statistics confirm the fall before anyone explains it
questions.explanation: Composition, window, instrument, and calendar effects are the cheap and common explanations, and a program that opens with a strategy debate about a data defect wastes a quarter of goodwill. Stop at the first check that explains the movement.

questions.question: A connector is built on one shared service credential so the pilot can start faster. What problem does that design create?
options: The assistant answers slowly, because every request is re-authorized against the same account
Usage reporting becomes unreliable, because all questions arrive under one identity
The assistant can reach records that the person asking is not allowed to open
The connection fails whenever the credential owner is unavailable or changes roles
questions.explanation: A shared credential carries whatever access the account holds rather than the access of the person asking, so the assistant can surface records a user cannot open. Mirroring each user's permissions is the safer default, and a connection that cannot refuse a request is not ready.

questions.question: A team wants to move a use case from reading curated documents to writing records in a system of record within a month. What does the integration ladder require?
options: The move is allowed once the vendor confirms that the write path is supported and documented
One rung per quarter, and only after the use case shows value at the rung it occupies
The climb is allowed if the writing step is limited to internal records rather than customer ones
The two rungs may be combined when the same team owns both of the connected systems
questions.explanation: Integration is a ladder, and each rung multiplies both the value and the blast radius, so a use case earns the next rung by demonstrating value at the one it holds. Climbing two rungs in a single push is how a pilot becomes an incident.

questions.question: Three candidate connections compete for one quarter of engineering time. How should they be ordered?
options: By announced business value, largest first, so the program can show results early
By the size of the team that requested each one, so the loudest need goes first
By reversibility of the worst likely failure first, then by the population that benefits
By technical difficulty, easiest first, so that the team builds confidence before harder work
questions.explanation: Rank by how easily the worst likely failure can be undone: read-only connections to curated content go first, and writes to anything leaving the company go last. Then weigh how many people benefit and whether the connection removes a step rather than adding one.

questions.question: A roadmap item needs a capability the team does not yet have, and nobody owns the work to build it. Where does the item belong?
options: In the run lane, so that the team keeps using what it already has while its skills improve
In the won't do lane for this year, because a prerequisite with no owner is a wish
In the prove lane with a capped budget, so that the gap gets tested rather than assumed
In the committed portfolio, with the missing capability treated as an assumption
questions.explanation: Every item consumes capability, so an item that needs a level the team lacks gets a dated prerequisite in the build lane with a named owner. Without an owner the prerequisite will not arrive, which makes the item a wish rather than a plan.

questions.question: A team is already mid-way through a major platform migration when an AI rollout is proposed for the same quarter. How should the roadmap treat the AI work?
options: Approve it and shorten the pilot, since the migration is a separate program
Approve it but add a communication campaign so that the team understands why both changes matter
Approve it in the run lane, where it counts as maintenance rather than change
Plan it against the capacity left after committed changes, which may push it to a later quarter
questions.explanation: Committed changes such as a platform migration consume the same absorption budget the AI program needs, and the roadmap is planned against the capacity that remains. The fix for saturation is sequencing, not more communication.

questions.question: Why should a pilot's kill criteria be written when it is approved rather than when it disappoints?
options: It moves the decision onto a number agreed in advance, so that stopping is not an argument
It guarantees the metric will hold, because everyone knows the threshold from the start
It removes the need for a named decision maker, since the numbers decide on their own
It lets the pilot skip the business case entirely, because thresholds replace the financial analysis
questions.explanation: A metric, a threshold, and a date agreed at approval move the weight of the decision from the person who championed the idea to a number nobody has to argue about later. Stopping then costs a decision rather than a fight.
